title: Adaptive fanout throttle and kernel-interleave hotfix for token-emission stalls
creator: Asha Kapoor
description: Summary: Multiple customers reported sudden TTFT regressions and a 20-60% drop in tokens/sec for mixed-variant workloads across Hosted, Dedicated and Private clusters after rolling runtime scheduler v1.18. Symptoms include long first-token latency spikes (~2-6s for some requests), sustained token emission stalls mid-stream, and uneven throughput across tenants. This ticket coordinates the urgent patch, customer communication, and follow-up engineering work to prevent recurrence. It consolidates triage notes, temporary mitigations applied, root cause hypothesis, and an action plan for a safe rollout to all environments.
reproduction_steps: 1) Send parallel chat requests (20 concurrent) to a model route that is configured to fan out to two variants: quantized-int8 and fp16. Use priming context ~1.5k tokens.
2) Observe first-token timeouts or 2-3s TTFT for 10-30% of requests in Hosted and Dedicated; Private clusters show higher variance depending on KV cache hit rates.
3) Run synthetic load with mixed short/long sequences to reproduce tokens/sec backpressure and intermittent mid-stream stalls.
4) Reproduce is more likely when prefix caching is enabled and kernel-selection heuristic prefers small-stride kernels that thrash when model weights are in different memory layouts.
mitigation: - Immediately gated the new scheduler heuristic on production (feature flag rollback) for all Hosted clusters at 2026-03-12 19:40 UTC.
- Deployed a temporary KV prefetch circuit breaker to prevent aggressive prefetching from overwhelming eviction queues (hosted/dedicated only) at 2026-03-12 21:15 UTC.
- Enabled a priority-aware fanout throttle that limits simultaneous variant fanout for the affected routes to 2 per-worker at 2026-03-13 02:30 UTC.
- Applied per-tenant soft-fallback: when tokens/sec drops below threshold, requests are routed to the stable variant (fp16) to restore throughput.
- Opened customer bridge and posted interim status for impacted customers; advised short-term mitigations (reduce concurrent primed requests; disable aggressive prefix caching).
root_cause_summary: Interplay between the new scheduler kernel-interleave heuristic and aggressive KV prefetching caused frequent micro-evictions and memory-layout contention on GPUs hosting mixed quantized and non-quantized model variants. The heuristic favored kernels that gave slightly better latency in isolation but caused repeated cache thrash under mixed fanout, increasing context warmup and stalling token emission. Prefetch bursts amplified the effect by filling eviction queues and stalling weight loads for alternate variants.
rollback_plan: If hotfix causes regressions, immediately re-enable the previous stable scheduler, disable KV prefetch for affected clusters, and revert fanout throttles to prior limits. Rollback steps are documented in the incident runbook and executable via the ops playbook (links below). Target rollback time < 10 minutes for hosted, < 30 minutes for dedicated/private with manual approval.
rollout_plan: 1) Validate hotfix in staging with heavy mixed-variant fanout tests (48h soak). 2) Canary deploy to 5% of Hosted traffic for routes flagged as high-risk. 3) Monitor TTFT/tokens/sec/SLOs for 2 hours, then progress to 25% and 100% if stable. 4) For Dedicated and Private, ship as opt-in config toggle; coordinate with SEs for customer-specific rollouts. 5) Schedule gradual removal of temporary circuit breaker after kernel selection is improved.

follow_up_actions: 1) Build microbench harness that simulates mixed-variant fanout with prefix caching and KV prefetch toggles.
2) Implement a more conservative kernel-selection fallback that considers current eviction pressure and live memory layout signatures.
3) Add TTFT and tokens/sec SLO alerts by model-variant and by tenant; surface top-10 routes contributing to degradation.
4) Document recommended route configuration for customers using mixed quantized variants (Console UX doc + API warning).
5) Include the hotfix and regression tests in release notes and CS playbook; schedule Dedicated/Private patch windows with customers.
